• Common names: Hong Kong crabs or Cheerleading crabs
  • Scientific name: Ptychognathus barbatus
  • Minimum tank size: 20 litres
  • Breeding: Very difficult
  • Optimal KH: 2–6
  • Optimal TDS: 150–200
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: omnivore / algae eater
  • Temperament: peaceful (less aggressive than many other crabs)
  • Life span: up to 1 year
  • Colour: yellow-brownish with spots

Description: the crab gets its name from the little hair tufts growing from its pincers. It is small, with a carapace usually 15–25 mm; some aquarists say full-grown crabs may be a little over 2.5 cm. The carapace is very broad and the legs long and slender. The body and legs are pale yellow or pale brown (various speckled shades) with brown setae (hair). The body colour changes frequently and often matches the surroundings.

Lifespan: no official data. In captivity, according to reports, they do not live more than 1 year.
The species is found in Taiwan, China, Japan, New Caledonia, Indonesia, the Philippines, Malaysia, India, Comoros and Madagascar.
They dwell near the mouth of a narrow river, hidden among the gaps between pebbles or rocks in calm freshwater springs at a depth of 0.2 m.
Freshwater Pom Pom crabs do not need a large aquarium. A small colony can be kept in a tank of at least 20 litres as long as it is fully cycled and heated.

There is very little information about proper husbandry for this crab, and many reports contradict each other. There is no unanimous opinion among aquarists, and the natural water parameters are not known. Most keepers say their care is almost identical to Neocaridina (cherry shrimp).

Some aquarists keep them at pH 6.4–7.2 and believe this is optimal, but nobody knows for sure. It is also difficult to say how hardy these crabs are, because their lifespan in the wild is unknown. Careful acclimation is needed.

Because they are burrowers, they need a sand or fine gravel substrate. They like to burrow underneath stationary objects to hide, so provide enough of those and enough soft sediment for sufficient territory and ground to burrow under.

Escape risk: the crabs climb extremely well, which is one of the main reasons people lose them. Secure the tank: seal the top completely, lower the water level and hide any cords, or they will crawl out.

Molting: like all crustaceans, they need to molt (shed the old exoskeleton) to grow. After shedding, while the body is still soft and flexible, they pump their bodies with water and increase in size. Molting is the most important and most dangerous process for them, as without a shell they are extremely vulnerable. To prevent predation, they dig burrows and molt there. If they disappear for a day or two, they are most probably molting. They need calcium to mineralize (harden) the shell.

Plants: there are no reports that Pom Pom crabs eat live plants or cut them down, so they are plant safe in this sense, unlike crayfish. However, they enjoy digging and might dig up finer rooted plants from the substrate. The best option is floating plants or tough plants with a solid root system.
Most keepers recommend: pH 7.0–7.2 (optimal 6.8–7.2, tolerated 6.2–7.6), GH 6–8, KH 2–6, TDS 150–200, temperature 22–28°C, nitrate below 20 ppm.

Freshwater Pom Pom crabs are omnivores and eat about anything edible they come across. Although they lean towards the herbivore side, they occasionally need protein-rich frozen foods (such as bloodworms, live brine shrimp, etc.). They are great scavengers and eat algae and detritus in the tank.

Because of their tufts, some people think they are a sort of filter feeder (like vampire shrimp or bamboo shrimp). In fact, they do not intentionally use their pom poms to filter the water column; they simply do not sit motionless in one place that long. However, they will eat anything that gets stuck in them.

They also readily accept fish or shrimp pellets, flakes and algae wafers. Do not forget a calcium supplement.

Many guides warn to avoid any food or plant fertiliser containing copper in any form. This is an exaggeration: all crustaceans need some copper because it is an essential part of their blood, and the concentration of copper in food is too small to hurt.

They have fascinating behaviour and personality. Freshwater Pom Pom crabs are extremely active and not timid at all. Unlike Thai micro crabs (Limnopilos naiyanetri), which you will rarely see again, you will often see them running quite fast around the perimeter of the tank.

Males can spar with each other at times, but they usually do no damage. Towards other inhabitants they are pretty much completely peaceful and do not seem to care about anything else in the tank.

Although fully aquatic, they can function on land as well. They go around and seek out the tallest place to stand, where they can stay out of water for a while. They love to burrow and use their claws to push the sand like a little bulldozer.

Tankmates: they show no aggression except for the occasional short squabble with their own species. They can even be kept with shrimp such as bamboo shrimp, cherry shrimp and Amano shrimp without losses. If you see a Pom Pom crab eating a shrimp or fish, it was already dead. They may pick fights with fish over food, but nothing serious. Shrimp usually retreat. Potentially, they can attack very small snails.

They are small and might easily fall prey to hungry tankmates. Choose only peaceful fish and avoid anything that could fit a crab in its mouth.

Sexing is easy but you have to see the underside. On the underside of the shell there is a V-shaped section, which differs in shape and size between males and females.

Males also have a fat pair of claws with a tuft of bristles at the "wrist" joint (the pom poms); females do not. Large females can have some tuft, but it is very feeble. Female claws are distinctly smaller and much narrower than those of males. In general, males are slightly bigger than females.

They live in freshwater rivers, but their larvae need brackish or saltwater for development. Nothing else is known about their reproduction. Ptychognathus barbatus larvae are only mentioned as having several (at least two) zoea stages and a megalopa stage. The duration of the stages is unknown, and there is no information about larval requirements or diet. There are no reports of successful breeding in captivity.

The Pom Pom Crab (Ptychognathus barbatus) is a fully aquatic freshwater crab (do not confuse it with the marine species that goes by the same name). These crabs are a true rarity and quite new to the hobby.

Freshwater Pom Pom crabs are very cute, friendly and small creatures. They are one of the least aggressive crab species in the aquarium hobby, which makes them suitable for nano tanks.

Unfortunately, there is not much information about them. No official studies of this species could be found, so their biology, ecology, behaviour and reproduction are not known. Besides basic taxonomy, science has not studied the Pom Pom Crab at all. Nonetheless, people already keep them in their tanks. The only way to find out more was to ask aquarists who keep or kept them.

The freshwater Pom Pom crabs are appreciated by fish and shrimp keepers for their peaceful nature and are a perfect addition to a community tank. A relatively recent addition to the hobby, they are quickly gaining popularity due to their peaceful nature and fun behaviour, which makes them a great option as tankmates for shrimp or small fish.
